title: Borel fixed point theorem for a solvable acting group
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness, connectedness and morphism properties have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-pc-morphism-conventions]. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. Let $H$ be smooth, connected and solvable. Let $X$ be a nonempty proper finite-type $F$-scheme, with an action $a:H\times_F X\to X$ satisfying the group-action identities. There is $x\in X(F)$ fixed scheme-theoretically by $H$: for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and every $h\in H(A)$, $a(h,x_A)=x_A$. The scheme $X$ need not be reduced or connected.

source.place: Corollary 17.3 (Borel fixed point theorem), p.353, from Theorem 17.1, p.352, and the orbit lemma 1.66; the theorem is for the solvable acting group, not for a reductive group.

proof.text: The scheme $X$ has a closed point by [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], since it is nonempty. By [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base], closed points are $F$-rational. The dimension of $X$ is finite by [lem-kun-dimension-finite-type]. For every $y\in X(F)$, [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] gives a nonempty locally closed orbit $O_y$. Its dimension is a nonnegative integer bounded by $\dim X$: chains in a subspace inject into chains of their closures in the ambient space, since intersecting back recovers each chain member. Choose $x\in X(F)$ for which $\dim O_x$ is least among these integers.

source.place: Corollary 17.3, printed p.353; orbit lemma 1.66, pp.27--28. Rational closed points: Stacks 0478 (varieties.tex, lemma-locally-finite-type-Jacobson) and 00FV (algebra.tex, theorem-nullstellensatz).

proof.text: Put $O=O_x$. The reduced orbit closure and its boundary $B=\overline O\setminus O$ are invariant, and every orbit in $B$ has smaller dimension, by [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry]. Because $O$ is locally closed, it is open in $\overline O$, so $B$ is a closed subset of $X$. If $B$ were nonempty, [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space] applied to this closed subset would give a point $y$ closed in $X$ and lying in $B$. It is $F$-rational by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base]. Then $\dim O_y<\dim O_x$, contradicting step 1. Hence $B$ is empty and $O$ is closed in $X$.

source.place: Corollary 17.3, printed p.353, closed-minimum-orbit argument; Corollary 1.66 and Proposition 7.5, pp.27--28 and 140.

proof.text: Give $O$ the reduced orbit structure supplied by [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry]. Since its support is closed, its locally closed immersion into $X$ is a closed immersion. It is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](c), and composing with $X\to\operatorname{Spec}F$ is proper by (a). In particular $O$ is a separated finite-type $F$-scheme. Write $K=H_x$ for the closed stabilizer subgroup scheme. The orbit map $q:H\to O$, $h\mapsto hx$, is faithfully flat by [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry]; $K$ is not assumed smooth.

source.place: Corollary 17.3 and Corollary 17.2, printed p.353; Proposition 7.4(b) and stabilizer definition, pp.139--140. Stacks 01W3 (morphisms.tex, lemma-composition-proper); closed immersions are proper.

proof.text: The action identities give $q(hb)=q(h)$ for $b\in K(A)$, for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$. More precisely, $q(h)=q(h')$ holds exactly when $h^{-1}h'\in K(A)$, by the defining equation $K(A)=\{b:bx_A=x_A\}$ in [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry]. Thus the morphism $H\times_F K\to H\times_O H$ given by $(h,b)\mapsto(h,hb)$ has inverse $(h,h')\mapsto(h,h^{-1}h')$. Both formulas are scheme morphisms, obtained from multiplication and inverse on $H$; the second component of the inverse factors through the stabilizer fibre because $h^{-1}h'x_A=x_A$. The two composites are identities by the group laws. The fibre products have the universal property of [def-pc-fibre-product]. These verify the precise quotient hypotheses of the next step, on all test algebras rather than only on $F$-points.

source.place: Proposition 7.11, printed pp.141--142; the orbit-stabilizer quotient identification used in Corollary 17.2, printed p.353.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-solvable-homogeneous-proper-subschemes] with $G=H$, this closed subgroup $K$, $Q=O$, and $q$ from steps 3--4. Its hypotheses on $H$ are exactly the smoothness, connectedness, affineness, finite type and solvability in the item. Step 3 supplies properness of $Q$. Its final assertion gives $K=H$ as subgroup schemes. By the defining stabilizer equation in [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry], this means $a(h,x_A)=x_A$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $h\in H(A)$, as required. The orbit construction allowed nonreduced $X$ throughout and used no connectedness assumption on $X$.

source.place: Theorem 17.1, printed p.352, final assertion, applied to the closed orbit as in Corollaries 17.2--17.3, printed p.353.

proof_origin.place: Corollary 17.3, printed p.353, through Theorem 17.1 and the orbit lemma 1.66. The quotient identification in Corollary 17.2 is expanded using the explicit stabilizer equations.

Its explicit quotient data (faithfully flat finite-type q, K-invariant, with G×K ≅ G×_Q G) identifies Q with the fppf quotient G/K. K is arbitrary, as in the source. Steps checked against the cited statements. Step 1: Jacobson density applied to X gives a closed point, which is rational by the residue-field node; the dimension node is Lean-closed and serves as a tool; the orbit-geometry hypotheses (G smooth, connected, affine, finite type; X separated, finite type) all hold. Step 2: the boundary is closed in X because O is open in its closure; Jacobson on that boundary gives a rational point whose orbit has smaller dimension, contradicting the minimum. Step 3: the reduced orbit with closed support is a closed immersion, and proper-fp-permanence (c) then (a) makes it proper. Step 4 (elementary): O→X is a monomorphism, so q(h)=q(h') iff h⁻¹h'∈K(A); the inverse map is built from multiplication and inverse. Step 5: every hypothesis of the new node holds, giving K=H, which with the stabilizer equation is the item's conclusion. Nonreduced X is handled legitimately because the orbit node allows it. New node B1–B4 and B7 are OK; it is not a restatement of a clause of the item (D1). Tested on K=G, G_a/G_m with K=1, B₂/T ≅ A¹, and G_a/α_p in characteristic p.
